name: Fat Gripz / grip thickeners

image.caption: Can I improve my forearms? I welcome any help I can get from cheap, knockoff fat gripz! :p

lead: Fat Gripz are thick rubber sleeves that wrap around a barbell, dumbbell or handle to increase its diameter. People use them to work the hands and forearms harder and build bigger-looking forearms and arms.

A thicker handle reduces how well the fingers can wrap around it, which raises the demand on the grip muscles. One acute study of 15 resistance-trained men looked at muscle activation and strength; forearm size over time has not been tested in the sources reviewed.

paras: The sleeves slip onto the bar or dumbbell for exercises like curls, rows and pulls, and come off when not wanted. They are used alongside a normal training program, with any forearm growth building over weeks to months.
No adverse effects were documented in the sources reviewed. Because the grip is harder, people may find they can lift less weight on exercises limited by grip.

angle.text: Users attach thick rubber sleeves to bars and dumbbells to challenge grip and forearms for arm size. The thicker handle raises forearm demand and, over training, can add muscle. One acute study exists; none examine forearm size or appearance.

lead: Fat Gripz are thick rubber sleeves that slip over a barbell, dumbbell, cable attachment or handle to increase its diameter, making it harder to hold. Lifters use them to give the forearms and hands more work, and many add them to curls and pressing to chase bigger-looking forearms and arms. [1][2]

The maker, Fat Gripz Enterprises, markets them as a way to build bigger, stronger arms by recruiting more muscle fibres per rep and to raise grip strength so more weight can be handled on other lifts; it sells three diameters, about 4.5 cm, 5.7 cm and 7 cm. [2] Those are the company's own claims.

One acute study in 15 resistance-trained men measured strength and muscle activity with and without the sleeves. [1][3] Grip strength references list thick-bar holds among methods for training the closing grip. [4] No long-term trial of forearm or arm size has been found.
infobox: About 4.5 cm, 5.7 cm and 7 cm outer diameter [2]

paras: The sleeves are made of a dense rubber compound that the maker describes as a military-grade compound similar to heavy-duty rubber, and fit over standard bars, dumbbells, cable attachments, machine handles and bands; bevelled ends are made to fit angled E-Z bars. [2] The brand sells three outer diameters: Fat Gripz One at 1.75 in (4.5 cm), Pro at 2.25 in and Extreme at 2.75 in (7 cm), recommending the Pro for most people and the One for smaller hands or weaker grip. [2]

The idea of thickening the handle is older than the product. The maker's page says athletes and bodybuilders have used custom thick bars for decades, and the sleeves are a portable way to get the same effect on ordinary equipment. [2]

The sleeves are sold by Fat Gripz Enterprises, whose website carries a copyright range beginning in 2008. [2] The range as listed on the site comprises three sizes, Fat Gripz One, Pro and Extreme, with a bundle containing all three for progressing from the thinnest to the thickest, and it lists a ten-year warranty and a 60-day money-back guarantee. [2] The company states that the product is used in over 80 countries and is sold with colour variants of each size. [2]

Typical retail prices on the maker's page at the time of writing ranged from about 28 to 38 US dollars per pair, with the three-size bundle at about 90 dollars. [2] The maker describes them as a portable alternative to dedicated thick bars. [2]

A thicker handle reduces how far the fingers can wrap around it, so the hand cannot close as completely and the finger and forearm flexors have to work harder to hold on. [2][4] The maker says this activates more muscle fibres and raises grip strength, and it quotes trainer Charles Poliquin on thick-grip implements recruiting more motor units in the elbow flexors. [2] The maker's page does not name peer-reviewed studies for these claims, relying on testimonials and unnamed studies. [2]

The sleeves are sold for use across sports and training styles listed on the page, including CrossFit, strongman, mixed martial arts, arm wrestling, powerlifting and law enforcement and military training. [2]

The maker's site presents testimonials from strength athletes and coaches. These include the trainer Charles Poliquin, quoted as saying thick-grip implements recruit more motor units, the bodybuilder Phil Heath, quoted as saying they hit every fibre, and statements attributed to CrossFit athlete Sara Sigmundsdottir, weightlifter Dmitry Klokov and jiu-jitsu competitor Alexandre Ribeiro. [2] The page also names powerlifter Larry Wheels and arm wrestler Geoff Hale as users. [2] These are the company's published endorsements and are presented as promotional testimonials rather than study results. [2]

Resistance-training discussion around the product generally follows two lines. One treats thick grips as accessory work for the hands and forearms, which look bigger when the flexor muscles are developed. The other treats them as a way to vary arm exercises. The 2021 laboratory study, in which maximal loads were lower and forearm activity was higher with the sleeves, is the data point usually cited for the trade-off between more grip demand and a lighter load. [1][3]

On T Nation, lifters log fat-grip versions of curls, dips, bench work, farmer's pickups and wrist curls. One poster wrote that they can turn anything into an axle and described them as good for elbow health; another said they gave an even bigger arm pump during a triceps block; others log forearm blocks of wrist curls with the sleeves. [5][6][7][8]
A strongman logger noted a practical trick of placing them over band attachments so knurling does not wear them. [9]

A 2021 study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research by Krings and colleagues examined the acute effects of Fat Gripz on strength and muscle activation in 15 resistance-trained men. [1][3] Participants completed one-repetition-maximum tests on a barbell in the deadlift, bent-over row, upright row and concentration curl, plus pull-ups to failure, with and without the attachments, while surface electromyography measured eight upper-body muscles. [3]

With the attachments, maximal strength was lower in each exercise and pull-up repetitions decreased. [3] Muscle activity rose in the forearm and shoulder muscles but fell in upper-arm muscles during the deadlift, bent-over row and pull-ups, with no differences in the upright row or concentration curl. [3] The authors concluded that the attachments may increase neuromuscular activation, but that the lower loads they allow might be less effective for building strength; they suggested muscle length positions may explain the differences. [3]
No longer-term trials on forearm or arm thickness were found.
